Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty Images Spain Pressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donor Key government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for Hamas Timothy Pratt Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Attorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide who is currently imprisoned in Madrid and sought in extradition, have submitted a brief ahead of a decisive government meeting on the case. Meanwhile, Chambers’ partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, met last week with multiple members of the Spanish parliament to assert his innocence. The legal team’s arguments include that the US government has failed to identify specific acts of violence or damages personally attributable to Chambers and instead is seeking to criminalize acts linked to political protest. They also assert that at least one figure of US law underpinning the request – “conspiracy to commit riot” – has no equivalent in Spanish law, which would also help render the extradition invalid. FBI raided Spanish vacation rental of wealthy leftwing funder James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after his arrest Read more It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas. Chambers’ defense has submitted its brief to the government ahead of a meeting by Spain’s council of ministers expected to take place on 22 September. The council can decide whether or not to allow the US extradition request to proceed, based in part on an evaluation of supporting materials the Trump administration supplied to the government on 26 August. Under Spanish law, at this “administrative” stage, the 22-member council has the power to deny the request, before it reaches a “judicial” stage. The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group Hamas. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators gather at Puerta del Sol in Madrid during a rally demanding the release of the US activist Fergie Chambers and opposing his extradition to the US on 5 September 2026 Photograph: Richard Zubelzu/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Chambers’ team say he has been supporting humanitarian aid and other projects. The 41–year-old self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s additional charges of “international money laundering” don’t hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means. Chambers’ donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries for several years – including the Sameer Project, in Gaza. “It would set an alarming precedent in all of Europe if Spain allowed the Trump administration to criminalize offering vital humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people and defending their rights,” said Baltasar Garzón , the acclaimed human rights lawyer and a member of Chambers’ legal team. “That’s what Fergie has financed: humanitarian aid and support for people in a situation of great need,” said Garzón. “That’s not terrorism, according to Spanish and European legal standards.” Meanwhile, Schnabel has met with members of Sumar and Podemos – progressive political movements vital to the coalition government of the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – and has written a one-page letter to Sánchez asking him to make “the only morally acceptable decision”, that of denying extradition. Sánchez forms part of the council of ministers. Schnabel has not escaped scrutiny since her partner was detained on 10 July in Ibiza. On a recent trip to New York, the FBI pulled her aside at JFK airport and confiscated her phone, she said. Support for Chambers in the lead-up to the 20 September meeting has come from Ione Bellara, leader of Podemos, who opened the party’s quarterly meeting last Saturday with a statement opposing the extradition request, saying that Chambers was “on the right side of history” with his financial support of Palestinians in Gaza. Similarly, Sumar, the leftwing coalition that governs jointly with Sánchez’s Socialist party, filed a statement in Spain’s congress earlier this week urging the government to deny the petition, “given that the goal of the extradition request … is to criminalize, persecute or punish [Chambers] due to his political opinions, his public activity or his participation in political movements – in this case, in support of the Palestinian people”. Irene Montero, member of Podemos and Spanish representative to the European parliament, told the Guardian that “Our laws don’t contemplate the actions he is accused of … [and] we can’t become a subject of the United States.” Activists have held rallies in recent days in at least six cities across Spain in support of Chambers, with plans for more. Other shows of support from farther afield have included a petition delivered to the Spanish government signed by actors, academics, activists and others, including Richard Gere, Greta Thunberg and Angela Davis. In Tunisia, supporters of the Club Africain football team displayed banners and T-shirts at a recent match that read, “Free Fergie”. In Portugal, at Festa do Avante , one of that country’s largest cultural festivals, fans held up a banner saying: “Free Fergie – supporting Palestine isn’t a crime.” Schnabel told the Guardian last month that the $7.5m went to support Club Africain. Hamed Mbarek, one of the club’s supporters and an organizer of fans at last Saturday’s match, said Club Africain was “pro-Palestine” and that Chambers and the club had “synchronicity”. Chambers’ money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time. His views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”. Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have also brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.” He has also been a staunch critic of the US, telling a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.” Irene Zugasti helped organize rallies earlier this week and last weekend in support of Chambers in Madrid, Barcelona and several other Spanish cities. She sees the case as bigger than whether he is extradited or not. “If they go after Fergie, they’ll go after anyone … It’s a test – to see until what point European governments feel pressure from the United States.” Explore more on these topics Spain Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Sam Sirann/Glide Magazine Woodside Analysis Why is Woodside sponsoring Fremantle’s AFL team – and will the climate crisis shift the relationship? Jonathan Barrett Dockers supporters cannot buy a barrel of Woodside oil – but the fossil fuel company hopes to buy into fans’ loyalty Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Wed 23 Sep 2026 20.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 20.03 EDT Share When an oil and gas company buys logo space on an AFL jersey, it isn’t trying to convince fans to buy its products. Fremantle Dockers supporters cannot, for example, go to their local service station to buy a barrel of Woodside Energy oil or a canister of its liquefied natural gas. This differs from the way most companies’ sponsorship deals are designed to convince consumers to buy their hamburgers, drink their beer and bet on their platform. When Fremantle’s number one ticket holder, Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker, wore the team jersey with the Woodside logo covered on tour during his team’s finals push, it reignited demands to drop the oil and gas sponsor over its contribution to rising temperatures. This all raises an obvious question: if a fossil fuel producer doesn’t sell to the public, why spend millions putting its name on a footy jumper in the first place, and subject itself to public criticism? ‘Good feeling’ Companies like Woodside tend to sponsor sporting teams and community organisations to stockpile social capital, a reservoir of goodwill they can draw on to absorb the shock of inevitable public backlashes. Fossil fuel companies, in particular, want to retain strong public support as they rely on state and federal policymakers – and sometimes local councils – to expand and operate. Community-led opposition movements can frustrate their projects. This helps explain why extractive industries seek out highly visible sponsorship deals with the sporting teams closest to their operations. The Australian business arm of Indian conglomerate Adani, known as Bravus, sponsors the North Queensland Cowboys, positioning its brand alongside a regional club near its coalmine. Josh Wilson, the federal Labor MP for Fremantle, was also seen wearing the Dockers jersey with tape over the Woodside logo Prof Emma Sherry, dean of school of management at RMIT University, says companies that have “complex relationships” with local communities often direct money to sports because they hope to build on fans’ emotional loyalty to their favourite teams. “We often see that money go to the arts, and of course, we often see it in sport,” says Sherry, who specialises in sport management. “What the companies are trying to do is use people’s love for their team to create a similar good feeling towards the company.” None of this is in itself nefarious, as there’s an unwritten social contract that companies give back to the communities they work nearby. But the issue is complicated when the high-profile sponsor is at the forefront of the carbon-emitting business, and is trying to use sport and other community activities to change views. When Woodside and Fremantle renewed their long-term sponsorship deal at the end of 2024, the oil and gas company included an awkwardly worded claim that the two WA-based organisations both had a “focus on sustainability”. That position recently became harder to defend after Woodside scrapped its long-term emissions and clean energy targets . In response to the “Woodside, get off my chest” campaign calling for the sponsor’s removal, a company spokesperson said Woodside was committed to its partnership with the Dockers and was “looking forward to continuing our work together”. An investigation by climate communication charity, Comms Declare , found that major coal, oil and gas companies are reaching children through schools, museums, science centres, sporting clubs, and other youth programs. Many of the institutions that accept the companies’ funding are “operating under genuine financial pressure and are providing valuable services to children and families”, it found. With sponsorship of 47 programs – including having its name emblazoned on the surf singlets worn by kids in the beach “nippers” program run by Surf Life Saving Western Australia – Woodside features heavily in the report. ‘We’ll have to stop playing’ The link between fossil fuel companies and sport is not new; oil and gas company Santos is a major commercial partner of the Wallabies and energy company Alinta Energy previously served as one of Cricket Australia’s main sponsors. Yet fan unease is growing into a familiar backlash, much like the rising community resistance to promotional efforts by sports betting platforms. It’s AFL grand final week – why is everyone talking about ‘Wharfie Time’? Read more Just as big tobacco once felt indispensable to rugby league, large commercial deals can make fossil fuel companies seem untouchable, right up until the culture shifts and alternative sponsors step in. While the AFL grand final is forecast to be played in cool conditions on Saturday, large parts of Australia, including Victoria, have just emerged from their hottest winter on record . Sherry says that growing climate awareness, particularly among younger fans, is showing sporting codes how a changing climate threatens their future. “Sport relies on the natural environment to be successful. For example, we have heat policies, and if the temperatures keep going up, we’ll have to stop playing,” says Sherry. “It is one of those things that’s becoming increasingly visible, not just from a sponsorship perspective, but also people realising that, if I’m in a snow sport and the snow melts, then my sport doesn’t exist. “Or if I rely on grassy fields to play, and there’s a drought, I won’t be able to play.” Jonathan Barrett is Guardian Australia’s business editor Explore more on these topics Woodside AFL analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Football AFL NRL A-League Cricket Rugby union Tennis Cycling F1
